groups.title: Find your local information first
groups.blurb: No national site can tell you your frost dates or which varieties do well three streets away. These can.

items.name: Cooperative Extension Service directory
items.what: Every US state runs a free public gardening advice service through its land-grant university, staffed by people who know your county's soil, pests and frost dates.
items.why: This is the single most useful bookmark on the page. Most run a free helpline, many offer soil tests for $15 to $25, and their advice beats anything general — including ours.

items.name: NOAA average last spring freeze map
items.what: Interactive map of the date your chance of a freezing night drops below 50 percent, from weather-station records.
items.why: Your real frost date, rather than one inferred from a hardiness zone. Put it into our planting calendar and every window recalculates.

items.name: USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map
items.what: Enter a ZIP code, get your zone. Revised in 2023, so re-check one you looked up years ago.
items.why: Useful for choosing perennials and as a rough starting point. Remember it describes winter lows, not frost dates.

items.name: USDA Local Food Directories
items.what: Official searchable listings of farmers markets, CSAs, food hubs and on-farm markets near you.
items.why: Growers at a farmers market will happily tell you what does well locally. It is the fastest shortcut to local knowledge there is.

items.name: American Community Gardening Association
items.what: Directory and resources for community gardens across the US and Canada.
items.why: A plot in a community garden gives you experienced neighbours, shared tools and someone to water while you are away. Hard to beat in a first year.

items.name: Buy Nothing Project
items.what: Hyper-local gift networks where neighbours pass on things they no longer need.
items.why: Pots, tools, spare seedlings and leftover compost circulate constantly in spring. A genuinely good way to start a garden for almost nothing.

groups.title: Apps and online tools
groups.blurb: Worth having on your phone. We have not been paid to list any of these.

items.name: iNaturalist
items.what: Photograph a plant or insect and get an identification, confirmed by a community of naturalists.
items.why: The best free way to work out whether the beetle on your squash is a problem before you do anything about it.

items.name: Our planting calendar
items.what: Pick your zone or enter your own frost dates to see what to sow, start indoors or transplant each month.
items.why: Built to accept your real frost dates rather than guessing them from your zone.

items.name: GrowVeg Garden Planner
items.what: Drag-and-drop bed planner that handles spacing and crop rotation for you, with a free trial and a paid subscription after it.
items.why: Genuinely useful once you are planning more than one bed. Overkill for a first 4x8.

items.name: A notes app you already have
items.what: One note per season: what you planted, when, and what happened.
items.why: Not a joke, and not a product. Next February that note is worth more than any book or app on this page.

groups.title: Where to get seed
groups.blurb: All of these ship across the US and publish germination rates and days-to-harvest properly.

items.name: Your local seed library
items.what: Many public libraries lend seed for free, the way they lend books. Search your library's site for 'seed library'.
items.why: Free, and the varieties on offer are usually ones that already do well in your area.

items.name: Johnny's Selected Seeds
items.what: Employee-owned supplier used by market growers. Detailed growing information on every variety.
items.why: The variety notes are more useful than most gardening books, and free to read whether or not you buy.

items.name: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds
items.what: Very large heirloom and open-pollinated catalogue.
items.why: Where to look once you want varieties no garden centre stocks. Heirlooms can be less disease-resistant, so mix in a modern variety in year one.

items.name: Botanical Interests
items.what: Packets printed with sowing instructions inside and out.
items.why: The packets themselves teach you. Good choice for a genuine beginner.

items.name: Your state extension's vegetable guide
items.what: Nearly every extension service publishes a free regional vegetable growing guide as a PDF.
items.why: Written for your climate by people paid to be accurate, not to sell you anything. Start here before buying a book.

items.name: Our glossary
items.what: Plain-English definitions of the terms seed packets and guides assume you know.
items.why: If a guide loses you at 'harden off before setting out transplants', start here.

toolkit.title: The starter tool kit
toolkit.blurb: What you actually need in year one, and what to skip. Prices are 2026 US retail estimates and vary a lot by region.
skip: Tillers and cultivators — a garden fork does the job on a 4x8 bed
Kneeling stools, tool belts and aprons — nice, not needed
Seed-starting kits with domes and heat mats, unless you are growing peppers
Anything sold as a complete 'garden starter set' — usually four times the component cost with thin steel

items.name: Hand trowel
items.what: For planting seedlings and digging small holes.
items.buying: Get one forged from a single piece of steel. The failure point on cheap trowels is where the blade meets the handle.

items.name: Garden fork or spade
items.what: For loosening the top 8 to 12 inches of soil and turning in compost.
items.buying: A fork beats a spade in most soils and is far less work in clay. Check the handle is wood or fibreglass, not hollow tube.

items.name: Watering can or hose wand
items.what: For watering the soil without blasting seedlings out of it.
items.buying: A rose or wand head matters more than the vessel. A bare hose end will wash out a row of carrot seed.

items.name: Gloves
items.what: For weeding, handling compost and anything thorny.
items.buying: Nitrile-coated fabric gloves fit closely enough to handle seed. Leather is overkill for vegetables.

items.name: Pruning snips
items.what: For harvesting, thinning at soil level and cutting twine.
items.buying: Bypass snips, not anvil. Anvil blades crush stems instead of cutting them.

items.name: Soil thermometer
items.what: For knowing when soil is actually warm enough to sow.
items.buying: The cheapest one is fine. This is the tool that answers 'why did my beans never come up' before it happens.

items.name: Tomato cages or stakes
items.what: Support for tomatoes, installed at planting time.
items.buying: Buy sturdier than looks necessary. The flimsy conical cages sold everywhere collapse under an indeterminate tomato by August.

items.name: Garden twine
items.what: For tying plants to supports and marking straight rows.
items.buying: Jute or hemp so it can go on the compost heap at the end of the season.
